extracted.intended_audience: aspiring writers, biographers, essayists, and readers interested in standards of literary taste
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and evaluative principles for composing biography, judging literary works, and producing representations of nature (painting/description). Emphasizes veracity, usefulness, style, and the distinction between form (beauty) and other properties (rarity, usefulness, colour).

rubrics_metrics.name: Attend to invariable and general ideas of nature
rubrics_metrics.description: The painter, by attending to the invariable and general ideas of nature, produces beauty; by regarding minute particularities and accidental discriminations, he deviates from the universal rule and pollutes his canvass with deformity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer universal/central forms (the 'central form') over idiosyncratic details. Avoid exaggerating accidental peculiarities; minute particularities lead to deformity rather than beauty. (Given as explicit advice: attend to general ideas to produce beauty.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not assume universal standards of beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Custom makes, in a certain sense, white black, and black white; though habit and custom cannot be said to be the cause of beauty, it is certainly the cause of our liking it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that aesthetic preferences are often products of habit and custom; avoid asserting absolute, cross-cultural standards of beauty. Be cautious claiming a form is 'beautiful' universally—preferences may reflect familiarity, rarity, or association.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define 'beauty' precisely (confine to form)
rubrics_metrics.description: I have here considered the word 'beauty' as being properly applied to form alone. There is a necessity of fixing this confined sense; for there can be no argument, if the sense of the word is extended to every thing that is approved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using 'beauty' in criticism or description, distinguish form-based beauty from other approvals (rarity, usefulness, smell, colour). Misuse of the term blurs argument and evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not conflate novelty with beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Novelty is said to be one of the causes of beauty: that novelty is a very sufficient reason why we should admire, is not denied; but, because it is uncommon, is it, therefore, beautiful?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admiration for novelty should not be equated with the aesthetic quality of form. Separate admiration due to rarity or novelty from judgments about form and true beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer first-hand knowledge for biography (certainty/veracity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The writer of his own life has, at least, the first qualification of an historian, the knowledge of the truth; certainty of knowledge not only excludes mistake, but fortifies veracity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, prioritize autobiographical or first-hand testimony in biographical writing because it furnishes certainty and resists falsehood. Treat second-hand accounts with more suspicion, especially about motives and private sentiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize ordinary life and moral instruction over mere splendour
rubrics_metrics.description: The mischievous consequences of vice and folly... are best discovered by those relations which are levelled with the general surface of life... The writer should tell not how any man became great, but how he was made happy; not how he lost the favour of his prince, but how he became discontented with himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good biography (and moral narrative) shows practical lessons drawn from commonplace experiences, domestic life, and personal failings rather than focusing solely on conspicuous, extraordinary events. Aim to instruct or illuminate ordinary human conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid heroic decoration and excessive distance in biography
rubrics_metrics.description: He that recounts the life of another, commonly dwells most upon conspicuous events, lessens the familiarity of his tale to increase its dignity, shows his favourite at a distance, decorated and magnified like the ancient actors in their tragick dress, and endeavours to hide the man that he may produce a hero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not sacrifice fidelity for grandeur. Present the subject with familiarity and humanity; avoid artificially magnifying or distancing the person to create a false heroism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against authorial motive bias (friendship, hatred, gratitude, party)
rubrics_metrics.description: He that writes the life of another is either his friend or his enemy, and wishes either to exalt his praise or aggravate his infamy... The zeal of gratitude, the ardour of patriotism, fondness for an opinion, or fidelity to a party, may easily overpower the vigilance of a mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about and correct for motives that incline toward panegyric or vilification. Strive for impartiality; recognize how personal or political allegiances can distort judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize and correct for self-love in autobiography
rubrics_metrics.description: He that speaks of himself has no motive to falsehood or partiality except self-love... falsehood cannot appease his own mind, and fame will not be heard beneath the tomb.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Autobiographers should be alert to self-deception and self-justification; though self-reporting often has advantages in truth, it still requires self-scrutiny and honesty to serve posterity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compilation must add value (collect scattered materials usefully)
rubrics_metrics.description: Particles of science are often very widely scattered... He that collects those under proper heads is very laudably employed... But the collections poured lately from the press have been seldom made at any great expense of time or inquiry...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compilers and anthologists should not merely rehash existing works; their task is valuable when they organize scattered useful materials, bring obscure insights to attention, and facilitate others' learning. Avoid lazy compilation and plagiarism.

rubrics_metrics.name: An author's work should inform, delight, or amuse honestly
rubrics_metrics.description: He that teaches us any thing which we knew not before, is undoubtedly to be reverenced as a master. He that conveys knowledge by more pleasing ways, may very properly be loved as a benefactor; and he that supplies life with innocent amusement, will be certainly caressed as a pleasing companion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for one or more of these virtues: impart new knowledge, present it pleasingly, or provide innocent amusement. Works that accomplish none of these risk being useless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt to prevailing taste without sacrificing substance
rubrics_metrics.description: Truth like beauty varies its fashions, and is best recommended by different dresses to different minds... he that can accommodate himself to the reigning taste, may always have readers who, perhaps, would not have looked upon better performances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider audience and current tastes in presentation and tone, but avoid compromising intellectual substance or originality merely to please fashion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inform yourself before informing others
rubrics_metrics.description: They might take care to inform themselves before they attempt to inform others, and exert the little influence which they have for honest purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do adequate research and reflection before publishing. Even modest authors owe readers accuracy and honest purpose; superficial ignorance is an ethical and artistic failing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid gratuitous repetition and excessive production
rubrics_metrics.description: To exact of every man who writes, that he should say something new, would be to reduce authors to a small number... Yet, surely, there ought to be some bounds to repetition; libraries ought no more to be heaped for ever with the same thoughts differently expressed...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise restraint: do not produce or publish redundant variations of the same ideas. Value novelty and economy; avoid adding to the clutter of literature without substantive contribution.
